nameStory: Shrub lespedeza gets its 'bicolor' name from its lovely two-toned flowers that bloom in late summer. The purple and white petals create a striking contrast that makes this Asian native stand out in the landscape. The genus name Lespedeza honors Vicente Manuel de Céspedes, an 18th-century Spanish governor of East Florida who supported botanical exploration.
description: Shrub lespedeza is a medium-sized deciduous shrub that typically grows 3-6 feet tall and wide. Originally from eastern Asia, this member of the legume family has gracefully arching branches that create a fountain-like shape. In late summer, it produces masses of small pea-like flowers in purple and white, followed by tiny flattened seed pods. It's commonly planted as an ornamental but has escaped cultivation in some areas of New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pea-like flowers appear in late summer, each about 1/4 inch long with purple upper petals and white or pale pink lower petals. They cluster densely along the stems and have the classic legume flower shape with a banner, wings, and keel.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-part compound leaves (trifoliate) with oval leaflets that feel soft and slightly fuzzy underneath. The leaves are arranged alternately on the stems and have a fresh green color that turns yellowish in fall.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a rounded, fountain-like shrub with long, arching branches that often touch the ground at their tips. The overall shape is graceful and weeping, especially when loaded with flowers.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, flattened brown seed pods about 1/4 inch long that contain a single seed. The pods feel papery when dry and often persist into winter.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are green to reddish-brown and feel smooth to slightly ridged. Older stems develop thin, grayish bark that may peel slightly in strips.

habitat: In New England, shrub lespedeza is primarily found around homes, parks, and roadsides where it was originally planted as an ornamental. It occasionally escapes to disturbed areas, field edges, and woodland borders, preferring well-drained soils and full to partial sun. Look for it near older residential areas and abandoned homesteads where it may persist long after other plantings have disappeared.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in mid to late spring as small, soft green trifoliate leaflets. The shrub begins putting on its graceful arching growth during this season.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in late summer (August-September) when masses of purple and white pea flowers cover the arching branches. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn pale yellow before dropping, and small brown seed pods become visible along the stems. The pods often persist after leaf fall.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the distinctive arching, fountain-like growth pattern. Dried seed pods may still cling to the stems, and the smooth bark becomes more noticeable.

funFact: Shrub lespedeza is such a late bloomer that it's often called a 'September beauty' because it provides nectar for butterflies and bees when most other flowers have finished for the year, making it like a final feast before winter arrives.
confusionNotes: The three-part leaves might remind you of poison ivy, but shrub lespedeza's leaflets are rounder and softer, plus it grows as an upright shrub rather than a vine. Remember: 'Leaves of three, let it be' doesn't apply to this harmless legume with its distinctive arching shrub form and late-summer flowers.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being widely planted as an ornamental, shrub lespedeza can become invasive in some southeastern states, though this is less of a concern in New England's cooler climate. It's sometimes confused with native bush clovers, but most of our native Lespedeza species are much smaller plants that hug the ground rather than forming tall, arching shrubs.
compareHints: Among the many Lespedeza species, shrub lespedeza is unique in New England for its tall, shrubby growth habit - most other bush clovers in our region are low-growing or trailing plants. Its bicolor purple-and-white flowers also set it apart from native species like round-headed bush clover, which has cream-colored flowers, or violet bush clover, which is solid purple and grows much closer to the ground.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Round-headed bush clover stands out from its Lespedeza relatives by its distinctly round, compact flower heads - most other bush clovers have loose, elongated flower clusters or flowers scattered along the stems.
Among New England's bush clovers, hairy lespedeza stands out for its distinctly fuzzy, velvety texture covering the entire plant.
Among its bush clover relatives, violet bush clover stands out with its smooth (not hairy) stems and leaves, and its loose flower arrangement rather than dense round clusters.
Among New England's bush clovers, Chinese bushclover stands out for its silvery, densely hairy appearance and aggressive colonial growth habit.
Among New England's bush clovers, slender bush clover stands out for its delicate, wispy appearance with thin stems and small flower clusters.

Among its bush-clover relatives, tall bush-clover stands out with its reliably erect stems - round-headed bush clover has similar upright growth but denser, more rounded flower clusters, while violet bush clover and trailing lespedeza have more sprawling or leaning growth habits.
Unlike its upright relatives like round-headed bush clover or hairy lespedeza that can reach several feet tall, trailing lespedeza never gets off the ground.
Among its bush clover relatives, narrow-leaved bush clover stands out for its distinctly slender leaflets and preference for wet soils.
Among the bush clovers in New England, violet bush clover stands out for its distinctly purple-violet flowers - most of its relatives have white, cream, or very pale pink blooms.
Among the lespedezas, Thunberg's is unique for its dramatic weeping form - most other bush clovers in New England grow upright or spreading but not with these long, graceful drooping branches.
While most of its lespedeza relatives like round-headed bush clover and violet bush clover grow upright in bushy clumps, creeping lespedeza is the ground-hugger of the family.
Downy lespedeza stands out from other bush clovers in New England primarily by its extremely fuzzy, silvery appearance.
